File: /tmp/claude-10001/-ai-inventor-aii-data-runs-run-wfWEMjpWKygr-3-invention-loop-iter-2-gen-report-text-gen-report-text/866264b9-4b21-44de-9b05-00275136a18f/scratchpad/part1.md

# Iteration 2: the bare prompt, the two unreported arms, and bans that act through the prohibition sentence

## 2.1 Why this iteration ran what it ran

The review of iteration 1 was blocking, and most of its must-fix items concerned the record, not the analysis. Two of the three arms had been written off as "not delivered", yet both had left thousands of generations on disk. The ban arm had 4,360 bare-prompt generations, labelled but never executed. The temperature arm had its full grid and its seed rows, generated but unlabelled. The influence arm, the only one reported, had appended an output contract (a fixed function signature) to every prompt, and that contract appeared to create the two-idea menus on which every steering conclusion rested. On the bare prompt, the ban arm's open-task baseline had four ideas above 3%, not two. The review also found three problems with the steering claims. The claim that random directions raise idea entropy as much as targeted ones compared single targeted cells with individual random draws at half the sample size. The closest published steering papers had not been compared. And conclusion 5 ("bans are mostly ignored by this 3B model") was contradicted by the ban arm's own data.

The hypothesis was revised in response (title: "Temperature flattens ideas, context reorders them"). It drops the claim that flattening the idea utilities is the creativity knob, and it moves every core test to the user's bare prompt. It also recasts a prompt ban as a displacement of an internal idea state rather than a restriction of the choice set. It states four testable claims, which we refer to by name throughout this section:

- the *temperature law*: the log-odds of each idea against the modal idea are linear in 1/T, the top-3 ideas never swap rank for T ≤ 1.3, and within-idea phrasing diversity rises at least 3 times faster with T than between-idea diversity;
- three ban claims: the *regularity test* (a ban can lower the share of an idea it does not name, which a model where the ban only removes options cannot produce); the *substitution-prediction test* (a predictor built only from internal geometry predicts where banned mass goes, at least 20% better in Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) than independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA), with the correct top substitute in at least 70% of single bans); and the *transplant test* (adding the ban's internal displacement to a placebo run reproduces at least 50% of the ban's effect, against at most 15% for random displacements);
- the *seed-shock test*: random seed strings act as small displacements, and the greedy flip rate they cause can be predicted within ±0.10, with under 5% flips on the weighted task;
- the *off-menu-correct test*: a ban or an internal displacement reaches a share of correct off-menu programs at least 3 times that of the best temperature, at no less than 0.8 times the baseline pass rate.

We define *off-menu correct share* as the fraction of programs that pass the execution oracle and implement an idea outside the task's baseline menu (ideas at 3% or more in the baseline). On textbook tasks a correct algorithm that a judge does not recognise is near-floor by construction, so this share replaces judge-confirmed invention as the novelty observable.

The hypothesis also imposed screening discipline. Existing data (the ban arm and the influence arm) are the screen. Predictors, layers and thresholds are fixed and hashed on the screen before any confirmation sample exists. Confirmation uses conditions never generated before: rank-5 to rank-8 single bans, random ban pairs, fresh seed strings, a reserved fourth task (k-th smallest element, T4) and a second model family (gemma-2-2b-it [20]), all on fresh sample seeds.

Three artifacts were planned and ran, one per block of claims:

1. **A shared label space plus the temperature and seed questions** [ARTIFACT:art_qJbC6mPQUr_5]. This artifact relabelled every bare-prompt program with one audited classifier, executed all of them, and wrote up the ban arm. It also fitted and froze the temperature law on the iteration-1 grid and tested it on a fresh 3,615-generation re-draw, and froze a seed-shock predictor before generating 2,160 programs under 120 new seed strings. It was chosen first because it answers the user's questions (a), (b) and (c), the seeding question and the ban question from data that already existed, at almost no GPU cost.
2. **Bans as displacements** [ARTIFACT:art_e6bJAhbt41cu]. This artifact read the ban's displacement from the prompt-final residual stream, fitted seven one-parameter predictors of where banned mass goes, froze them, and scored them on 5,930 never-generated confirmation generations including T4. It then ran the causal transplant and drew the idea manifold the user asked for.
3. **Selection versus flattening on the bare prompt, and a second model** [ARTIFACT:art_wQJ_kngaEEa6]. This artifact re-analysed iteration 1's random-control claim against draw-averaged random entropy, and ran a pre-registered select-or-flatten test of a difference-in-means "away from the default idea" direction on Qwen with 5 random draws per strength. It then repeated the ban-prediction, temperature and transplant tests on gemma-2-2b-it, with Gemma Scope sparse autoencoders [19] as a descriptive last step.

The model remains Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct [1] unless gemma is named. Tasks: T1 is the open path-search task, T2 the sorting task (`Implement a sorting algorithm`), T3 the weighted shortest-path task and T4 the k-th-smallest task. All bare-prompt work uses the ban arm's wording (`Implement a path search algorithm in Python`, `Implement a sorting algorithm`, `Implement a function that finds a shortest path in a weighted graph`, with no system prompt beyond Qwen's default and no output contract). We call this the *ban-arm wording*. The iteration-1 temperature grid used a slightly different wording, which we call the *grid wording*: a final full stop, "in Python." added to T2, and a longer T3 sentence that names non-negative edge weights. Section 2.5 shows that this small difference matters. A *placebo* is the bare prompt followed by a prohibition of an irrelevant algorithm (`Do not use the Rabin-Karp algorithm.` on T1 and T3, `Do not use Kruskal's algorithm.` on T2). Every ban is compared with the placebo, never with the plain baseline, because the placebo sentence alone shifts the idea distribution. A ban sentence has the form `Do not use X.`, `Do not use X or Y.` or `Do not use X, Y or Z.`.

## 2.2 Corrections made in place to iteration 1

The review's points about the record were fixed where they point, each marked as a correction in Sections 1.2, 1.4, 1.9, 1.10, 1.12, 1.16 and 1.17. In summary: the two "not delivered" arms are restated with their actual output; every influence-arm conclusion is marked as conditional on the contract prompt; the "bans are ignored" claim is restricted to the contract prompt with list wording; the random-parity claim is replaced by the draw-averaged comparison of Section 2.9; the novelty-direction Spearman interval is replaced by an exact permutation p-value; and the file counts are corrected.

## 2.3 One label space for all bare-prompt programs

Iteration 1 used two classifiers that were never compared: the influence arm's AST classifier and the ban arm's rule classifier. The first artifact adopted the ban arm's rule classifier (hash `d0d321215bc2`, with its 45 fixture programs) as the single classifier for all bare-prompt programs, because it covers both graph and sorting ideas [ARTIFACT:art_qJbC6mPQUr_5]. It reproduced all 4,210 stored ban-arm labels exactly. Every program then ran through a sandboxed execution oracle that discovers the entry point and calling convention, since bare-prompt programs have no fixed signature. Graph tasks are checked against a reference BFS and Dijkstra on random graphs; sorting tasks on random arrays. Pass rates on the bare prompt are therefore not comparable with the contract-prompt pass rates of iteration 1. A share of failures are programs the oracle could not call (on the T1 baseline, 41 not callable and 38 load errors among 300).

The classifier was audited blind on a stratified sample of 200 programs by two LLM judges (gpt-4.1-mini and gemini-2.5-flash-lite) at a cost of $0.042. Agreement between the rule classifier and the first judge is high on sorting and the weighted task and moderate on the open task (Table 28). The judges agree with each other at kappa 0.92, which bounds what any classifier can reach. The influence arm's AST classifier agrees with the judge far less (kappa 0.53), and with the rule classifier at kappa 0.44 to 0.76 depending on the source, which confirms that labels from the two iteration-1 arms are not directly comparable. The rule classifier's main confusions with the judge were: {{audit_conf}}.

## 2.4 The iteration-1 ban arm, written up

The ban arm generated, for each task, a baseline (n = 300), a placebo and ten ban conditions (n = 100 each) at T = 0.7 under vLLM [22], plus forced-idea cells (`... using X.`, n = 10 per idea) and 50 co-mention lists (`List 10 algorithms that could solve this task`). Ranks refer to the baseline: on T1 rank 1 to 4 are BFS, DFS, A* and Dijkstra, and the rare idea is SPFA. All counts below are re-derived from the stored generations with the rule classifier and the iteration-2 oracle [ARTIFACT:art_qJbC6mPQUr_5].

**The contract made the menu.** Table 29 sets the two iteration-1 baselines side by side. On the open task the bare prompt gives four ideas above 3% and 1.76 bits of idea entropy, against two ideas and 1.15 bits under the contract. On the weighted task the bare prompt gives Dijkstra in 300 of 300 programs, while the contract gives a BFS-style queue relaxation in 71 of 300. Part of this gap could be labelling, since the arms used different classifiers. The comparison nonetheless shows that the two-idea menus of Section 1.4, the rank-1 erasure and the explanation that flattening "overshoots the uniform point" all depend on the contract.

The HF and vLLM baselines agree within sampling noise (JSD 0.009 on T1 and 0.001 on T2, chi-square p 0.18 and 0.91) [ARTIFACT:art_wQJ_kngaEEa6]. The answer to the user's question "does the model always design BFS?" is therefore prompt-dependent. Under the bare prompt it writes BFS in 60% of programs, DFS in 15%, A* in 13% and Dijkstra in 7%. Under the contract it writes BFS in 68% and DFS in 27%.

**Compliance is high on the bare prompt, and substitution is structured.** Tables 30 to 32 hold every ban-arm condition. Banning BFS on T1 leaves 1 of 100 programs using BFS and moves the mass to DFS (66 against 17 under the placebo). Banning DFS gives BFS 98 of 100. Banning Dijkstra raises A* from 1 to 34. Banning the top three (BFS, DFS, A*) or the top five ideas produces iterative deepening DFS (IDDFS) in 42 of 100 programs, an idea that never appears in the baseline and that combines the two banned searches. Non-compliance rises with list length: on T1, 1, 29 and 38 of 100 programs still use a banned idea under the top-1, top-3 and top-5 bans; on T3, 12, 46 and 61. This rise is what the priming account of negative instructions predicts [5]. On T2 compliance is near total (0, 0 and 7 of 100), and the top-5 ban yields counting sort 45 and heap sort 26, ideas outside the comparison-sort family that was banned. On T3, banning Dijkstra yields Bellman-Ford in 55 programs, 44 of them correct; banning A*, Bellman-Ford or Floyd-Warshall, none of which the model writes, leaves Dijkstra at 95 to 100.

Two features of these tables recur through the rest of the section. First, the placebo sentence alone moves the distribution: on T1, A* falls from 39 of 300 at baseline to 1 of 100 under the placebo, and on T2 bubble sort falls from 60% to 43%. Second, bans on T1 and T3 cost correctness. The T1 top-5 ban raises entropy to 2.54 bits, but the pass rate falls to 0.05 and 61% of outputs hit the token cap.

**Regularity violations already appear on the screen.** A ban that only removes options can raise but never lower the share of an unbanned idea. Table 33 lists the cells where an unbanned idea lost share against the placebo at Holm-corrected p < 0.05 (Fisher exact tests over 28, 34 and 26 cells). The largest are T2: banning insertion sort, which the model writes in 5% of baseline programs, takes bubble sort from 43 to 1, and banning quicksort takes it from 43 to 15. On T1, banning the rare SPFA takes DFS from 17 to 1. The replicate files the plan relied on for a noise floor do not exist, so the floor comes from splitting the baseline into thirds ({{noise_screen}}). Every listed drop exceeds that floor.

Table 33. Screen regularity violations: unbanned ideas that lost share under a ban, against the placebo (n = 100 each).

{{reg_screen}}

**Wording within the bare prompt matters little for one ban; the grid wording matters a lot for sorting.** Two paraphrases of the rank-1 ban (`Avoid using X.` and `Your solution must not use X or close variants of it.`) give distributions within JSD 0.012 to 0.054 of the plain ban (Table 34). They differ significantly only on T2, where the split between quicksort and merge sort moves. The grid wording, by contrast, moves the T2 baseline from bubble sort to quicksort as the mode (JSD 0.107, permutation p < 0.001). The temperature grid was therefore run on a different T2 distribution from everything else in this section.

Table 34. Wording checks: paraphrased bans against the rank-1 ban, and the grid wording against the ban-arm wording at T = 0.7.

{{wording}}

The forced-idea cells check that the model can write each idea when asked, and that the classifier recognises it (Table 35). Purity is 0.8 or higher for every sorting idea and for most graph ideas. The exceptions are greedy best-first search on T1 (0.5, the rest A*) and T3 (0.2), and BFS (0.5) and DFS (0.6) on T3, where a request for BFS or DFS on a weighted graph often yields SPFA or Dijkstra. With n = 10 per cell these purities are rough.

Table 35. Forced-idea cells (`<task> using X.`, n = 10 each, T = 0.7).

{{forced}}

The co-mention lists show what the model knows about each task, as opposed to what it writes. On T1 all 50 lists name BFS, DFS, Dijkstra and A*, 48 name bidirectional and greedy best-first search, and 29 name IDDFS (Table 36). On T2 every list names seven sorting algorithms. The menu the model writes from is far narrower than the menu it can list.

Table 36. Co-mention lists: how many of 50 lists (`List 10 algorithms that could solve this task`) name each idea.

{{comention}}

What the ban arm settles is behavioural. In this 3B model, at T = 0.7 and on the bare prompt, a short prohibition is obeyed in most programs. Banned mass goes to particular neighbours: DFS for BFS, A* for Dijkstra, IDDFS for the BFS/DFS/A* triple, Bellman-Ford for Dijkstra on weighted graphs, and non-comparison sorts when the comparison sorts are banned. Bans can also lower unbanned ideas. The geometry behind these moves is the subject of Section 2.8.

## 2.5 The temperature arm, labelled, and a frozen re-draw

The iteration-1 grid has 100 programs per cell over T in {0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3, 1.6} and top-k in {10, none}, with top-p = 1, on the grid wording, at a 768-token cap and one fixed base seed per sample index. The first artifact labelled and executed it, fitted the temperature law on it, and froze the fits (sha256 `d1dabe95…`) [ARTIFACT:art_qJbC6mPQUr_5]. It then generated a confirmation re-draw on the ban-arm wording: the same grid on T1 and T2, no top-k only on T3, seeds 1000 to 1099, and a 1,536-token cap to cut truncation. Tables 37 and 38 give every cell.

Idea diversity is measured with Hill numbers [11]. D0 is the number of distinct ideas, D1 the exponential of the Shannon entropy and D2 the inverse Simpson index. The *expected ideas among 10* is the rarefied number of distinct ideas in a random draw of 10 programs, which is the user's question about "10 reasoning trajectories" read off directly. *Within-idea diversity* (alpha_1) is the order-1 similarity-sensitive diversity of programs inside one idea, computed on normalised code with edit-distance similarity in rarefied draws of 8 programs per idea and averaged over ideas. *Between-idea diversity* (beta_1) is the ratio of total to within-idea diversity.

Table 37. Temperature grid, grid wording (n = 100 per cell, 768-token cap). Unparseable outputs count as a class in the entropy here, which is why the T = 1.6, no top-k cells show nonzero entropy with almost no code.

{{cells_screen}}

Table 38. Temperature re-draw, ban-arm wording (n = 100 per cell, 1,536-token cap, seeds 1000..1099).

{{cells_redraw}}

[FIGURE:fig_temp_bare]

**Temperature adds ideas slowly and breaks code fast.** On the open task (re-draw, no top-k) idea entropy rises from 1.70 bits at T = 0.3 to 1.96 at T = 1.0, while the pass rate falls from 0.49 to 0.19. At T = 1.3 a third of outputs are "other", mostly incomplete code, and at T = 1.6 almost nothing parses. Top-k = 10 keeps T = 1.6 usable (pass 0.06 on T1, 0.82 on T2), but it does not add ideas beyond what T = 1.0 already gives. Sorting is the one task where heat buys ideas at little cost: entropy rises from 0.74 bits at T = 0.3 to 2.00 at T = 1.0 at pass 0.99. Even there, the new mass goes to the same five comparison sorts. The weighted task stays at Dijkstra up to T = 1.0, and above that the extra entropy comes from broken output, not from new algorithms.

**The temperature law fails as stated.** Table 39 gives every fitted line of idea log-odds against 1/T, and Table 40 the multinomial-logit fits with a curvature test. Table 41 applies the pre-registered criteria. No task-and-top-k combination meets all of them, on either draw. Three findings matter more than the binary verdict.

First, R² ≥ 0.85 is a weak criterion at n = 100 per cell. A simulation from a truly linear law with the observed shares gives R² below 0.85 in 25% to 87% of draws (Table 42). The curvature likelihood-ratio test is the better check. It does not reject linearity on the grid for T1 (p 0.97 and 0.97) and rejects it weakly for T2 without top-k (p 0.034). On the re-draw it rejects linearity only for T1 without top-k (p 0.016).

Second, the T1 intercepts are significantly below zero, for example A* at −2.38 [−3.19, −1.56] on the grid. A pure temperature-scaling model, in which each idea has a fixed utility and T only divides the utilities, predicts zero intercepts. Some ideas therefore lose ground at every temperature for reasons that 1/T does not capture. Lines for A* and, on the re-draw, Dijkstra are flat in 1/T: their share relative to BFS does not change with temperature.

Third, rank reversals among the top three occur at T ≤ 1.3, but only among the minority ideas (A* against DFS on the T1 grid; DFS against Dijkstra on the re-draw; quicksort against bubble sort at T = 1.3 on the T2 grid, not significant). The mode never changes below T = 1.6.

Table 39. Fitted lines of idea log-odds (against the modal idea) versus 1/T, weighted least squares, on the grid and the re-draw. "Rest (pooled)" pools all other classes including unparseable output and is not part of the criteria.

{{arrhenius}}

Table 40. Multinomial-logit fits with a curvature likelihood-ratio test (linear vs quadratic in 1/T).

{{glm}}

Table 41. Pre-registered criteria of the temperature law, per draw and task. The within/between slope ratio compares the slope of ln alpha_1 with the slope of ln beta_1 against T; the law requires at least 3.

{{criteria}}

Table 42. Simulation under a true linear law with the observed shares (200 simulated grids per line): how often R² falls below 0.85, and how often the curvature test falsely rejects.

{{sim}}

**Ideas against phrasings: the answer to the user's questions (a), (b) and (c).** Table 43 gives the diversity partition and Table 44 the "10 trajectories" view. At T = 0.3 on the open task, 10 programs contain about 2.4 (grid) to 3.5 (re-draw) distinct ideas and 8 to 9 distinct phrasings (normalised code at edit-distance similarity below 0.85). The model gives a few ideas, each in many phrasings, even at the tightest temperature; that is the user's case (a). Case (b), ten ideas with one phrasing each, never occurs: the largest expected number of ideas among 10 in any cell is 4.9 (T2, T = 1.6, no top-k, where a third of outputs are unparseable). As T rises the number of ideas grows slowly (T1 re-draw: 3.5 to 3.9 from T = 0.3 to 1.0) and phrasings saturate at 10 of 10 by T = 1.0. Sorting differs. At T = 0.3 bubble sort is written almost identically every time (2.7 distinct phrasings among 10), and heat adds both ideas and phrasings, with between-idea diversity rising faster than within-idea diversity (slope ratio 0.58 to 0.79). Phrasing grows at least 3 times faster than ideas in no cell; the largest ratio is 2.64, on the T1 re-draw.

Table 43. Diversity partition: log within-idea (alpha_1) and log between-idea (beta_1) diversity per temperature, with slopes against T.

{{hill}}

Table 44. The user's "10 trajectories" view: expected distinct ideas and distinct phrasings in a random draw of 10 programs. A cell is labelled (a) when it has at most 3 ideas and at least 7 phrasings, (b) when it has at least 7 ideas, and mixed otherwise. The last row of each block is the change from T = 0.3 to 1.3 with the verdict for the user's case (c).

{{abc}}

**Out of sample, the frozen law helps on T1 and hurts on T2.** Table 45 scores the frozen grid fits on the re-draw against two baselines. One is fixed utilities, in which the T = 0.7 shares are raised to the power 0.7/T. The other is no temperature effect at all. On T1 with top-k 10 the frozen law has a mean absolute error of 0.040 against 0.073 for fixed utilities, and without top-k 0.109 against 0.129. On T2 it loses (0.100 and 0.103 against 0.028 and 0.056). The T2 loss is largely the wording change: the grid was fitted with quicksort as the mode and the re-draw has bubble sort as the mode, so the frozen ordering is reversed at every temperature.

Table 45. Out-of-sample scoring of the frozen temperature law on the re-draw (mean absolute error over ideas and temperatures, calibration slope in brackets, and mean JSD per cell).

{{oos}}

Correctness depends on the idea as well as on temperature (Table 46). On T1, Dijkstra programs pass most often (0.53 grid, 0.65 re-draw) and A* least often (0.04, 0.09). Each unit of T lowers the log-odds of passing by 1.7 to 4.6. Top-k 10 raises the pass rate on T2 (coefficient 1.25 to 1.40, p ≤ 2e-5) and slightly on the T1 re-draw.

Table 46. Pass rate by idea, and the effect of T and top-k on passing (logistic regression over all cells of a draw).

{{correct}}

**Truncation and reproducibility.** Half of the grid rows (51.1%) stopped at the 768-token cap. Truncation is more likely at high T, for A* (odds ratio 182 against BFS) and for Dijkstra (7.7). The audit continued 150 truncated rows from their own tokens (Table 47). Labels flipped in 16 of them (10.7%). Most flips were bubble sort becoming merge sort: the model writes a short bubble sort as a first example and then a merge sort, and the classifier labels the final program. Regenerating 20 rows under vLLM reproduced none of the 768-token prefixes; the median common prefix was 2 tokens. The user's "always the same seed" protocol is therefore not bit-reproducible under vLLM batching, although 17 of 20 repeated rows kept their label.

Table 47. Truncation audit and reproducibility.

{{trunc}}

## 2.6 Seed strings narrow the ideas

The user asked whether prepending a random seed string helps. The iteration-1 seed rows used 60 strings per task of the two forms the user gave, a random-character string (`seed=` followed by 11 random characters, as in `seed=d32qxk4nt43`) and four random words (as in `seed=(horse chair roof love)`). The user's two literal strings were not among them. The first artifact froze a predictor of the greedy flip rate (sha256 `1cffcec3…`) [ARTIFACT:art_qJbC6mPQUr_5]. The planned internal readout, the model's log-probability of each idea's name token, failed its pre-registered coverage gate on T1 and T2 (prefix coverage 0.10 to 0.37). The behavioural fallback was therefore primary: a Gaussian-shock model fitted to the screen's greedy flips. The artifact then generated 120 fresh strings per task (60 of each kind) on the ban-arm wording, with one greedy sample and five samples at T = 0.7 each.

**The seed-shock test fails.** The frozen prediction matches the observed greedy flip rate on T1 (0.28 predicted, 0.25 observed) and on T3 (0.00 and 0.00, under the 5% bound), but not on T2 (0.39 predicted, 0.017 observed) (Table 48). The T2 miss traces to the wording change. On the grid wording the unseeded greedy program is quicksort, and seed strings flipped it to bubble sort in 88% of cases. On the ban-arm wording the unseeded greedy program is already bubble sort, and seeds keep it there. Random words flip T1 far more often than random characters (0.42 against 0.08).

Table 48. Greedy flips under 120 fresh seed strings per task, against the frozen prediction.

{{seed_flip}}

**Seeds lower idea diversity.** At T = 0.7, seeded samples have lower idea entropy than unseeded ones on T1 (−0.34 bits [−0.53, −0.13]) and T2 (−0.68 [−0.92, −0.47]) (Table 49). Random words on T2 cut entropy by more than a bit and push 282 of 300 samples to bubble sort. Seed strings make the model more predictable: they push it toward the modal idea rather than away from it. T3 does not move at all (597 of 600 Dijkstra).

Table 49. Idea diversity of seeded and unseeded samples at T = 0.7 (5 samples per string; unseeded n = 300).

{{seed_div}}

Table 50. Non-mode share, heterogeneity between strings, and the intraclass correlation of the mode.

{{seed_t07}}

The narrowing is not because seeds leave the residual stream untouched. At the last five chat-template tokens, a seed string displaces the residual stream 1.5 to 3 times more than a ban sentence on T1 and T2 at most layers (Table 51), and the seed displacement is nearly orthogonal to the ban displacement (mean cosine between −0.20 and 0.13 across layers). On T3 the ban displaces more than the seed at layers 24 and above. A large displacement in an irrelevant direction does not change the idea; the ban's smaller displacement does. Section 2.8 shows that even the ban's displacement at these positions is not where the ban acts.

Table 51. Norm of the residual displacement at the last five chat-template tokens (mean over tokens), by layer: seed string against unseeded prompt, ban against placebo, and placebo against plain baseline.

{{seed_disp}}

## 2.7 The temperature reference for off-menu correct programs

The off-menu-correct test needs a temperature comparator. The first artifact froze it before the sibling artifacts used it (sha256 `783778b0…`) [ARTIFACT:art_qJbC6mPQUr_5]. The rule picks, per task and source, the temperature with the highest off-menu correct share among cells whose pass rate is at least 0.8 times that at T = 0.7. No temperature produces more than 8% off-menu correct programs on any task (Table 52). On T1 the best is SPFA in 2 of 100 programs; on T2 it is insertion sort, which is just below the 3% menu threshold at baseline; on T3 it is zero.

Table 52. Frozen temperature reference for the off-menu-correct test (menus: T1 BFS, DFS, A*, Dijkstra; T2 bubble, quick, merge and selection sort; T3 Dijkstra).

## 2.8 Bans as displacements: what the internal state predicts, and what it does not carry

**Design.** The second artifact asked whether the internal change a ban sentence causes predicts which ideas gain share, and whether that change causes the behaviour [ARTIFACT:art_e6bJAhbt41cu]. We define the *ban displacement* Δh as the residual-stream difference between the ban prompt and the placebo prompt. It is read at the five chat-template tokens that end every prompt (`<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>assistant\n`), which are aligned across conditions, and averaged over layers 32 to 34. That band was chosen by a per-layer idea probe against shuffled labels. Probe accuracy was nearly flat across all 35 layers (balanced accuracy 0.72 to 0.74), as in iteration 1, so the band choice carries little information. Idea centroids come from a *commitment window*, the mean residual over the 17 generated tokens starting at the first token that names or implements the idea (or the first 32 generated tokens when no such token is found), computed on baseline and forced-idea programs. The forced cells were extended by 810 new generations to 40 per idea.

Seven predictors of the post-ban idea distribution share one floor-and-compliance model and differ in one scalar each. They were fitted by leave-one-ban-out on the 27 screen bans and frozen by sha256 and git commit before any confirmation generation:

- *IIA*: proportional renormalisation (the Luce rule) of the placebo distribution over the unbanned ideas;
- *displacement*: each idea's log-share shifts by β times the projection of Δh onto that idea's centroid direction (β = 19.75, near the edge of the pre-registered grid);
- *nested geometry*: substitution weighted by centroid cosine similarity, as in the iteration-1 plan;
- *name embedding* and *prompt embedding*: the same substitution weights read from bge text embeddings [21] of the algorithm names and descriptions, or of the prompt difference;
- *Qwen name embedding*: weights from Qwen's own input embeddings of the names;
- *co-mention*: weights from how often two ideas appear together in the co-mention lists.

Confirmation used 5,930 never-generated vLLM generations at n = 100 per condition. On T1 and T2 these were rank-5 to rank-8 single bans and six random ban pairs per task; on T3, bans of SPFA and BFS. There were also three placebo blocks per task, an alternative placebo, a cross-domain ban, "You may use X" mention controls, and the whole of T4 as pure transfer: baseline, forced cells, co-mention lists, rank-1 to rank-4, top-3, top-5 and rare bans, and four pairs. T4 needed its own classifier and oracle, audited by gpt-4.1-mini on 60 programs (kappa 0.79, $0.015). The placebo P0 used for confirmation is the mean of the three placebo blocks: {{p0}}.

Table 53 gives every confirmation condition with its observed counts and the JSD of four of the frozen predictors.

Table 53. Confirmation conditions (n = 100 each, never generated before the predictors were frozen), with the JSD between observed and predicted distributions.

{{conf}}

**The regularity test passes.** In 8 of 46 tested cells an unbanned idea lost share beyond the noise floor at Holm-corrected p < 0.05, spread over 6 of the confirmation bans (Table 54). Testing placebo blocks against each other in the same way gives 0 violations in 45 cells, and shuffling ban and placebo labels gives 0 in each of 20 repetitions. The most striking cases are bans of ideas the model almost never writes. Banning greedy best-first search, written in 0 of 300 placebo programs, takes A* from 3% to 58% and BFS from 63% to 23%. Banning IDDFS, also absent, gives A* 49%. Banning Bellman-Ford takes Dijkstra from 5% to 56%. On T2, banning radix, counting or shell sort, none of which the model writes, takes bubble sort from 54% to between 15% and 28%. A ban that only restricted the choice set could not move mass between ideas it does not name. These bans act more like an instruction to "do something other than the obvious", and the model's answer is a particular other idea.

Table 54. Confirmation regularity violations (placebo = three pooled placebo blocks, n = 300).

{{reg_conf}}

**The substitution-prediction test fails, narrowly on the primary criterion and clearly on the top-substitute criterion.** On the 22 T1 to T3 confirmation bans, the displacement predictor has a mean JSD of 0.188 against 0.207 for IIA, a 9.2% reduction (95% CI [−0.6%, 19.6%]) against a required 20% (Tables 55 and 56). Its top predicted substitute is right in 20% of bans against a required 70%. It does predict the sign of share changes well: on the 52 cells where an idea moved by at least 10 points, it is right in 83% (balanced 0.79), where IIA can only predict gains (0.65, balanced 0.50). It also beats both bge text-embedding predictors and the co-mention predictor on T1 to T3 (all CIs exclude 0), so the internal state carries information about substitution that the names alone do not. On T4, pure transfer, it is 25% worse than IIA (CI [−102%, −0.5%]), and across all 33 bans the reduction is 2.8% (CI [−9.1%, 12.8%]). Anchoring the displacement predictor on the screen placebo instead of the confirmation placebo lowers its JSD to 0.165, with a top-substitute hit rate of 0.35 and sign accuracy of 0.84. Part of the error is therefore the placebo itself drifting between draws.

**The transplant test fails, and decoding-time attention to the ban sentence restores the placebo behaviour.** The artifact added Δh to the placebo run at the five suffix tokens at layer 32 during prefill, with common random numbers and n = 60 per cell, for six screen bans. *Recovery* is 1 − JSD(patched, ban) / JSD(placebo, ban). Mean recovery is −0.001, the same as 5 matched-norm random displacements (−0.006) (Table 60). Subtracting Δh from the ban run restores nothing (0.01). Overwriting the suffix residual at all 35 layers, which forces the whole prompt-final state to equal the ban's, recovers 0.01 and 0.04 on the two bans tried. Adding Δh at every prompt position, in the style of Stolfo et al. [17], recovers 0.08 and −0.03. Patching at layers 8 and 18 does no better. An exploratory cell then knocked out attention from every generated token to the ban sentence's tokens during decoding. That restored the placebo distribution with a mean restoration of 0.72 over four bans (0.57 to 0.80). The ban is read from the sentence tokens while the program is being written, not from a summary state at the end of the prompt. The plan's causal claim about the prompt-final idea state is therefore dead, while the claim that the ban acts through attention to the sentence is supported by one exploratory manipulation.

**No priming in the suffix displacement.** Decoding Δh through the unembedding (logit lens) gives top tokens such as ` while`, ` although`, ` rather`, ` another` and ` nouvel`, plus rare multilingual tokens; the banned name ranks in the thousands to tens of thousands (median best rank 17,600 over 26 screen bans) (Table 62). The one exception is banning DFS on T1, where `DFS` ranks 72 at the band and first at layer 35. That is also the ban with the most extreme outcome (BFS 98 of 100). The suffix state says "do something else"; it does not prime the banned name, so the priming account of non-compliance [5] does not act at these positions.

**Edge or far side: no consistent direction.** The user asked whether, after the top ideas are banned, mass moves to the edge of the banned region or to the opposite side. The *edge statistic* compares the internal similarity between the post-ban mass and the banned centroids with what the placebo mass would give; positive values mean the mass lands near the banned ideas. On the screen it is positive for most T1 bans (BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, the top-3 and the rare ban: 0.14 to 0.29) and negative or near zero for T2 and T3 (Table 63). No single statistic reaches permutation p < 0.05 except the first paraphrase on T1 (p 0.029). The top-5 bans are near zero on all three tasks (−0.035, 0.006, 0.003). Overall {{edge_sum}}. The same statistic from text embeddings is near zero everywhere. Bans on path search send mass to internal neighbours of the banned ideas; bans on sorting do not; top-5 bans do neither in a measurable way.

**The manifold.** The user asked for a map of the path-search ideas with each centroid sized by how often the model implements it. The artifact projected commitment-window activations at the band layers onto principal components per task and wrote the coordinates to its results files (Tables 64 to 66). The structure is driven by ideas, not by surface features: the idea label explains 77%, 82%, 57% and 28% of PC1 variance on T1 to T4 (eta²), and no surface feature explains more than 17% (output length, truncation, number of headers, prose before code, a main guard). On T1, PC1 separates the shortest-path family (Dijkstra at 33.8, SPFA 23.1, Bellman-Ford 63.6, Floyd-Warshall 68.4) from the unweighted searches (BFS −27.9, DFS −24.7, IDDFS −26.1). PC2 separates the heuristic searches (A* 38.6, greedy best-first 37.9, bidirectional 33.3) from the rest. BFS, the default, sits next to DFS and IDDFS, which is where its ban sends mass. Under the top-5 ban the mean point moves from (−26.2, −7.7) at baseline toward the upper middle (−12.4, 6.4), between the heuristic cluster and the IDDFS/DFS cluster; it does not cross to the far shortest-path side. Section 1.10 had noted that iteration 1's PCA view showed a 70-unit spread along PC1 not aligned with idea labels. That view used the contract prompt and a different window. On the bare prompt PC1 is label-dominated.

## 2.9 Steering on the bare prompt: selection confirmed, flattening not seen, and a second model

### 2.9.1 Iteration 1's random-control claim, re-analysed

The third artifact first re-analysed the influence arm's random-control comparison as the review required [ARTIFACT:art_wQJ_kngaEEa6]. Each of the 18 targeted settings at the five survival strengths (three per knob family and task) was compared with the mean entropy of the three random draws at the same strength. The comparison used Miller-Madow-corrected entropy on n-matched seeds 0 to 74 and a hierarchical bootstrap that resamples draws, then samples within draws. Three settings beat the draw mean, five are significantly below it and ten are undetermined (Tables 67 and 68). The below-mean settings are the difference-in-means and probe-weight directions on the open task, which select DFS; the settings above the mean are the novelty direction at α = 0.632 on the open task and the difference-in-means direction at α = 0.224 and 0.473 on the weighted task. With only three random draws at n = 75, draw-level variance is poorly estimated, so most comparisons cannot be resolved. The statement that random directions raise idea entropy as much as targeted ones is withdrawn. The defensible statement is that, where targeted directions select, they lower entropy below random, and elsewhere the data cannot separate them.

Table 67. Iteration-1 targeted settings against the draw-averaged random entropy (primary specification: Miller-Madow, n-matched seeds 0..74).

{{claim3}}

Table 68. How the verdict depends on the specification (counts out of 18 targeted settings).

{{claim3_counts}}

The novelty-direction dose-response is not significant by exact permutation (Table 69).

Table 69. Exact permutation test of the novelty direction's Spearman correlation between strength and atypicality (6 strength points).

{{a4}}

**How this compares with published steering results.** The selector finding agrees with the reliability literature. Tan et al. [13] find that steerability varies widely across inputs and that steering vectors can fail on some concepts. Turner et al. [7] report that a matched-norm random vector barely changes outputs. Our iteration-1 random draws did change the idea mix, by up to 0.6 bits in single draws, but the draw-averaged re-analysis no longer supports parity. Olson et al. [14] extract a direction from "boring" against "creative" prompts and report that adding it raises the creativity of text. That is close to our cross-task novelty direction, which transferred perfectly as a readout (AUROC 1.0) but did not raise atypicality monotonically in code (Table 69). STARS [15] and Riemannian activation steering [16] report diversity gains over plain sampling. They do so by optimising several steering directions jointly across concurrent generations at test time, which is a different intervention from one fixed direction. What this run adds to these comparisons is execution-verified correctness, algorithm-level labels in place of lexical diversity, five matched-norm random draws per strength, and a fresh-seed re-draw. Candidate reasons for the disagreement with the creativity-steering results are the task (code with a small menu of textbook ideas, not open text), the model size (3B), the late layers (29 to 34 of 36), and the window of the first 64 generated tokens.

### 2.9.2 Select or flatten: the pre-registered test on the bare prompt

**Design.** On the bare prompt, with menus of four or more ideas, a direction that flattens and a direction that selects make different predictions. A flattener lowers the mode share without making any single other idea dominant, so the distance from uniform falls steadily with strength. A selector hands most of the mass to one other idea. The artifact built the *away-from-mode direction* as the difference in means of commitment-window activations at layers 32 to 34 between non-modal and modal programs, unit-normalised per layer. It added the direction at the prompt-final token and the first 64 generated tokens with strength α times the layer's median residual norm divided by three, as in iteration 1. Comparators were five matched-norm random directions per strength, an off-target real direction (the other task's away-from-mode direction), temperature 1.0 and 1.3, directions toward the centroids of two off-menu ideas (IDDFS and Bellman-Ford on T1, counting and heap sort on T2), and simply asking for those ideas. The frozen rules (sha256 files) were:

- strength s1: the α whose mode share is closest to half the baseline mode share;
- strength s2: the α with the lowest mode share whose pass rate stays at least 0.8 times the baseline's (calibrated on n = 30);
- SELECT: at s2 one non-modal idea takes at least half the samples, that idea was a predicted gainer, and the distance from uniform rises again from s1 to s2;
- FLATTEN: the distance from uniform falls from baseline to s1 to s2 and no non-modal idea reaches half the samples.

Predicted gainers came from two frozen rankings. One is the projection of the away-from-mode direction onto each centroid's offset from the mode; the other is each centroid's nearest-neighbour similarity to the modal centroid. On T1 the {{pred_T1}}. On T2 the {{pred_T2}}. Main runs used seeds 0 to 149 and a re-draw used seeds 1000 to 1149, both on the HF engine.

**Result: SELECT on both tasks, replicated on both draws.** On T1 at s2 (α = 0.224), BFS falls from 61% to 13% and A* rises to 57% (main) and 63% (re-draw). A* was the projection ranking's top predicted gainer. None of the five random draws makes A* the top gainer, and they leave BFS at 61% to 72%. The non-mode share is 0.54 above the random-draw mean [0.47, 0.61]. The cost is correctness: the pass rate falls to 0.17 against 0.34 for the random-draw mean, below the 0.8 bar the n = 30 calibration had predicted, and 78% of outputs hit the token cap. On T2 at s2 (α = 0.473), bubble sort falls from 62% to 1% and 0%, and quicksort rises to 65% and 68%, again the projection ranking's prediction, at a pass rate of 0.92. T2 entropy at s2 is 0.71 bits below the random-draw mean [−0.94, −0.44], the signature of selection. On T1 entropy at s2 is above the random mean on the main draw (+0.32 [0.04, 0.56]) and undetermined on the re-draw (+0.10 [−0.19, 0.36]), because the T1 baseline mode is so dominant that moving mass to A* while keeping BFS, DFS and Dijkstra at 13% to 15% each raises entropy even though one idea takes over. The nearest-neighbour ranking (IDDFS on T1, selection sort on T2) was wrong on both tasks. The direction lands on the idea along its own projection, not on the idea that sits closest to the mode.

Some random draws also move T2 a lot: draw 3 at s2 gives selection sort 72 of 150, and draw 0 gives quicksort 75. The random-draw mode share at s2 ranges from 0.19 to 0.69. A single random cell would have misled either way, which is why the comparison is against the mean of five draws.

### 2.9.3 The second model: gemma-2-2b-it

The plan reserved gemma-2-2b-it [20] for confirmation. The third artifact ran it on the HF engine with eager attention, at sample sizes cut for a 16 GB GPU: baseline n = 150, three placebo blocks of 50, forced cells of 20, bans of 50, temperature cells of 40 and transplant cells of 30, with a 768-token cap. The gemma classifier audit (100 programs, gpt-4.1-mini, $0.020) gives {{g_audit}}. Gemma's T1 labels are flagged as label-limited, and 87% of its T1 answers hit the token cap.

**The baselines differ from Qwen's.** Gemma's T1 baseline is split between A* (49) and BFS (48), with Dijkstra 27 and DFS 15; its T2 baseline is bubble sort 121 of 150 (Table 77). The placebo sentence alone moves gemma's T2 mode from bubble sort to merge sort (about 55% across blocks). The placebo noise floors are large (18 points on T1, 12 on T2), so the T1 confirmation is underpowered. Gemma obeys bans on T2 almost perfectly and barely on T1: under the top-3 ban (A*, BFS, Dijkstra) BFS still appears in 36 of 50 programs.

Its top-substitute hit rate is 7%. It predicts the same substitute for nearly every ban, and the independent re-check finds that scoring it against a mismatched ban's prediction does no worse. On gemma, the prompt-final displacement is dominated by a generic "do not use" component. On the screen it ties IIA (0.249 against 0.254) and wins only where gemma ignores the ban. Regularity holds in 71 of 72 cells; the exception is the heap-sort ban on T2, where merge sort falls from 0.55 to 0.16 (Holm p 7e-5).

## 2.10 What iteration 2 established, and what it did not

**Established.**

1. *The default answer is a mode, not an average, and it depends on the prompt's wording.* On the bare prompt the open-task default is BFS (60%), with DFS, A* and Dijkstra as a stable minority. The menu is four ideas wide, not two. Adding "in Python." to the sorting prompt changes the mode from bubble sort to quicksort, and the influence arm's output contract had narrowed the path-search menu to two ideas.
2. *Temperature is a weak idea knob and a strong correctness knob.* It adds ideas slowly, never changes the mode below T = 1.3 (one within-noise tie on the T2 grid), and does not follow a pure scaling law. Its most useful range for ideas is T ≤ 1.0, where idea entropy rises by 0.3 bits on paths and 1.3 bits on sorting. Even at T = 0.3 the model writes 2 to 3.5 ideas per 10 programs, each in many phrasings, which is the user's case (a). Case (b) never occurs.
3. *Seed strings narrow ideas.* Prepended random strings make the model pick its mode more often (−0.34 and −0.68 bits at T = 0.7), although they displace the residual stream more than a ban does.
4. *Bans are displacements of behaviour, not restrictions of a menu.* On the bare prompt bans are mostly obeyed; they lower the shares of ideas they do not name, and banning ideas the model never writes moves the whole distribution. The internal displacement at the prompt's end predicts the sign of share changes (83%) and beats text-embedding predictors, but it does not beat IIA by the required margin, and on gemma it loses to IIA.
5. *The ban is not carried by the prompt-final state.* Transplanting, subtracting or overwriting that state does nothing on either model. Blocking attention from the generated tokens to the ban sentence restores the placebo behaviour. The ban is applied while the program is being written.
6. *Internal directions select.* On menus of four or more ideas, the away-from-mode direction hands most of the mass to the one idea its projection predicts (A* on paths, quicksort on sorting), replicated on fresh seeds, against five random draws that do not. It never flattened. Off-menu ideas are reached by asking for them; steering toward their centroids fails except for heap sort.
7. *Off-menu correct programs.* They are rare at every temperature (at most 8%) and are reached on sorting by bans and by the heap-sort direction (up to 90%). On path search no knob tested reaches them beyond 1 in 100.

**Dead ends recorded as such.**

- *The temperature law as pre-registered.* Killed by Tables 41 and 45: no task meets all criteria on either draw, the T1 intercepts reject pure scaling, and the frozen law loses to fixed utilities on T2 out of sample. Linearity in 1/T itself survives the curvature test on most lines, and gemma T2 is near-linear.
- *Seeds as shocks whose effect can be predicted from a utility gap.* Killed by Table 48 (T2 predicted 0.39, observed 0.017) and by the failed readout gate. Seeds narrow rather than diversify.
- *The prompt-final idea state as the carrier of a ban (the transplant test).* Killed on both models by Tables 60 and 83: recovery about 0 against random displacements about 0, with a 35-layer overwrite also at about 0.
- *Internal geometry as the best predictor of substitution.* Killed as stated by Tables 55 and 80: 9.2% better than IIA on Qwen (20% required), 20% top-substitute hits (70% required), worse than IIA on T4 and on gemma.
- *Nearest-neighbour geometry as the predictor of where steering lands.* Wrong on both tasks (IDDFS and selection sort predicted, A* and quicksort observed).
- *Random-direction parity (iteration-1 conclusion 3).* Withdrawn by Tables 67 and 68.
- *Bans are ignored by this model (iteration-1 conclusion 5).* Withdrawn by Tables 30 to 32; true only under the contract prompt with list wording.
- *Steering toward an off-menu idea's centroid as a novelty knob.* 0% to 1% target share for three of four ideas (Table 74).

**Not settled.**

- Whether the commitment to an idea happens at a single token. Forking-path resampling [4] has still not been run in any iteration.
- How the ban sentence is read during decoding. The knockout is one exploratory manipulation on four bans; which heads carry it, and at which generated positions, is unmeasured.
- Why the same displacement predictor that ties IIA on Qwen loses on gemma. Gemma's weaker compliance on T1 and its larger placebo shifts are candidates.
- All results are from one wording per condition, and Qwen results from one model size.

## 2.11 What the next iteration takes from this one

The open question is now mechanistic and narrow: where, during generation, does the model read a prohibition or a request and turn it into an idea? Iteration 2 showed that the prompt-final state does not carry it and that attention to the instruction tokens during decoding does. The next step is attention-head-level activation patching on the knockout cells, located with forking-path resampling. That would show where the idea is fixed relative to the moment the model reads the instruction. A second, cheaper step is to test the selector result on the wording variants that moved the mode (grid wording against ban-arm wording) and on gemma, where it has not been run.

## 2.12 Bookkeeping

- **Artifacts.** `art_qJbC6mPQUr_5` (gen_art_experiment_4): 13,968-program ledger; new generations: 3,615 re-draw, 2,160 fresh-seed, 150 truncation continuations and 20 regenerations; about 2.5 h on one NVIDIA L4 (23 GB); judge spend $0.042. `art_e6bJAhbt41cu` (gen_art_experiment_5): 810 forced-extension and 5,930 confirmation generations under vLLM, 71 transplant cells (4,260 HF generations); about 3 h on one L4; judge spend $0.015. `art_wQJ_kngaEEa6` (gen_art_experiment_6): 9,720 Qwen and gemma generations on the HF engine; about 4.5 h on one RTX 2000 Ada (16 GB); judge spend $0.020. Total paid calls this iteration: $0.077.
- **Frozen files.** Temperature law `d1dabe95…` (2026-10-16); seed predictor `1cffcec3…`; off-menu reference `783778b0…` (frozen 03:40:12 UTC); ban predictors frozen 2026-10-16 03:07:25 with git commit `9336da7a`, centroid hashes per task; Qwen selector rules and strengths (two sha256 files); gemma ban predictor `7be800bb…`.
- **Deviations.** The ban arm's top-up replicate files did not exist, so the screen noise floor uses baseline thirds. The seed readout failed its gate, so the behavioural predictor was primary. Within-idea diversity used edit-distance similarity only (the planned code-embedding variant was skipped). The selector band is layers 32 to 34, not iteration 1's 29 to 31. The third artifact disabled its code-stop rule after a check showed it changed 13% of T1 labels, and discarded 400 early generations made with it. Gemma sample sizes were cut as listed in Section 2.9.3, and gemma ran without vLLM. The ban predictor's β = 19.75 lies near the edge of its grid.
- **Independent re-derivation.** Each artifact re-derived its headline numbers with separate code and placebo checks: label reproduction 4,210/4,210, judge kappas, Arrhenius slopes (exact match), out-of-sample errors, greedy flip rates, confirmation JSDs, regularity counts with 0 violations in 20 shuffled-label repetitions, sign accuracies, transplant recoveries, selector verdicts, the entropy-against-random differences (exact match) and the gemma confirmation comparison. The gemma comparison came out at −0.88 against −0.71 in the pipeline, because only the classes present were scored, with the same direction. Random draws tested against each other and shuffled targeted/random labels give CIs that include 0.
- **Kept on the run volume only, not in the published repository.** Activation caches of the second artifact (`acts/`, about 600 MB, regenerable) and of the third (`data/acts/`, about 200 MB), and the frozen vectors, centroids and displacements (`results/*.pt`).

A flattener lowers the mode share without making any single other idea dominant, so the distance from uniform falls steadily with strength. A selector hands most of the mass to one other idea. The menu is four ideas wide, not two. Adding \"in Python.\" to the sorting prompt changes the mode from bubble sort to quicksort, and the influence arm's output contract had narrowed the path-search menu to two ideas.\n2. *Temperature is a weak idea knob and a strong correctness knob.* It adds ideas slowly, never changes the mode below T = 1.3 (one within-noise tie on the T2 grid), and does not follow a pure scaling law. Its most useful range for ideas is T ≤ 1.0, where idea entropy rises by 0.3 bits on paths and 1.3 bits on sorting. File: /tmp/claude-10001/-ai-inventor-aii-data-runs-run-wfWEMjpWKygr-3-invention-loop-iter-2-gen-report-text-gen-report-text/866264b9-4b21-44de-9b05-00275136a18f/scratchpad/closing.md

# What we have learned so far

The run asks how an instruction-tuned model chooses the solution idea for an open design task, and whether that choice can be moved toward ideas the model does not usually produce. After two iterations the evidence comes from Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct [1] on four tasks (open path search, sorting, weighted shortest path, k-th smallest element) and from gemma-2-2b-it [20] on two. It rests on about 47,000 labelled and executed programs [ARTIFACT:art_aSN7z8WuA7Ir] [ARTIFACT:art_qJbC6mPQUr_5] [ARTIFACT:art_e6bJAhbt41cu] [ARTIFACT:art_wQJ_kngaEEa6].

**The default answer is the mode of a small menu, and the prompt's wording sets the menu.** Asked to implement a path search algorithm, Qwen writes BFS in about 60% of programs, with DFS, A* and Dijkstra as a stable minority. Asked for a shortest path in a weighted graph, it writes Dijkstra in 300 of 300. The model can list many more ideas than it writes: every co-mention list names BFS, DFS, Dijkstra and A*, and most name bidirectional and greedy best-first search. Small wording changes move the menu. An output contract narrowed path search to BFS and DFS, adding "in Python." changed the sorting mode from bubble sort to quicksort, and an irrelevant prohibition sentence (the placebo) cut A* from 13% to 1%. The user's picture of a range of answers from which the model returns the middle does not fit: the distribution is multi-modal over discrete ideas, and the model returns its mode.

**Temperature is not the creativity knob.** Raising T adds ideas slowly and breaks code quickly. On paths, idea entropy rises by about 0.3 bits from T = 0.3 to 1.0 while the pass rate halves, and the modal idea never changes below T = 1.6 except for one within-noise tie. Even at T = 0.3 a set of 10 programs holds 1 to 3.5 ideas, each in several phrasings; ten ideas with one phrasing each never occurs. That answers the user's questions (a) to (c) in favour of (a): tight temperature gives a few ideas in many phrasings, and loosening it adds phrasings first and ideas slowly. Top-k = 10 mainly keeps high temperatures from degenerating. The idea log-odds are roughly linear in 1/T, but the pre-registered temperature law fails: intercepts reject pure scaling, minority ideas swap ranks, and the frozen law does not transfer across a wording change.

**Seed strings make the model more predictable.** Prepending `seed=` with random characters or random words lowers idea entropy at T = 0.7 (by 0.34 bits on paths and 0.68 on sorting) and changes the greedy idea in at most a quarter of cases.

**Bans move behaviour, through the instruction tokens.** On the bare prompt a short `Do not use X.` is obeyed in most programs, and the freed mass goes to particular ideas: DFS when BFS is banned, A* or Bellman-Ford when Dijkstra is banned, IDDFS when BFS, DFS and A* are banned, and counting and heap sort when the comparison sorts are banned. Bans also lower ideas they do not name, and banning an idea the model never writes moves the whole distribution (banning greedy best-first search takes A* from 3% to 58%). Read as a choice model, bans violate regularity. The residual-stream displacement at the end of the prompt predicts the direction of these shifts (83% sign accuracy) better than text embeddings of the algorithm names. It does not predict the distribution much better than proportional renormalisation (9% against a required 20%), and on gemma it is worse. Transplanting that displacement does nothing on either model, while blocking attention to the ban sentence during decoding restores the unbanned behaviour. To the user's question of whether banning the top five sends mass to the edge or to the opposite side: on path search mass goes to the banned ideas' internal neighbours (IDDFS sits next to BFS and DFS), on sorting there is no consistent direction, and for top-5 bans the internal statistic is near zero on all three tasks.

**Internal directions select; they do not spread.** A difference-in-means direction pointing away from the default idea hands most of the probability to one other idea, the one its projection predicts: A* on paths (57% and 63% on two seed draws) and quicksort on sorting (65% and 68%). Five matched-norm random directions do not do this. No direction tested in either iteration flattened the idea distribution. Steering toward an off-menu idea's centroid fails for three of four ideas, while asking for the idea in the prompt succeeds in 92% to 100% of programs. Iteration 1's claim that random directions raise entropy as much as targeted ones does not survive a draw-averaged comparison.

**Novelty.** No condition in either iteration produced a correct program that a judge did not recognise as a known algorithm. On textbook tasks this metric is near-floor by construction. The informative quantity is the off-menu correct share. It stays at or below 8% for every temperature; on sorting it reaches 44% under a top-3 ban and 90% when steering toward heap sort, and on path search no knob tested exceeds 1 in 100. In these models, creativity as a behaviour means moving the model to another known idea. Bans, explicit requests and selective steering do that; temperature and seed strings do not.

Status of the user's questions after iteration 2:

1. *Is temperature the creativity knob, and do cases (a), (b) or (c) hold under tight temperature with top-k = 10?* Answered: no. Case (a) holds at every tested temperature on both models; ideas grow slowly with T while correctness falls; top-k = 10 caps degeneration more than it changes ideas (Sections 2.5 and 2.9.3).
2. *Does the model always design BFS for the path-search prompt?* Answered: BFS in about 60% of bare-prompt programs, with DFS 15%, A* 13% and Dijkstra 7%; the share depends on wording (Section 2.4). Gemma splits between A* and BFS.
3. *Does context seeding help?* Answered: no. Random-character and random-word seed strings of the user's form narrow ideas rather than diversify them (Section 2.6). The user's two literal strings were not themselves tested.
4. *Is the model giving the average answer?* Answered: it gives the mode of a multi-modal distribution over discrete ideas, and context (a ban, a mention, a wording change) moves it to a different mode rather than to a different part of a continuum (Sections 2.4 and 2.8).
5. *How much do prompt instructions matter?* Answered: more than any other knob tested. A one-sentence ban or mention moves the idea distribution by up to 95 points; "new algorithm" prompts change little, and long novelty prompts break the code (Sections 1.9, 2.4 and 2.8).
6. *What do the internals of BFS, DFS and Dijkstra runs look like, and can a manifold be drawn?* Partly answered. Commitment-window activations form a label-dominated map (idea label explains 77% of PC1 variance on paths) in which the shortest-path family, the unweighted searches and the heuristic searches separate (Section 2.8, Tables 64 to 66). Gemma Scope SAE features were tried and are unreliable on the instruction-tuned model; thought anchors and forking-path analysis have not been run.
7. *After banning the top ideas, does mass move to the edge or the opposite side?* Partly answered: to the banned ideas' internal neighbours on path search (IDDFS after banning BFS, DFS and A*), with no consistent direction on sorting and a near-zero statistic for top-5 bans (Section 2.8).
8. *Can we make LLMs give truly creative and novel solutions?* Answered for these models and tasks: no knob produced a correct program outside the known algorithms, and that metric is near-floor on textbook tasks. Bans, explicit requests and selective steering do reliably move the model to less typical known ideas, sometimes correctly; temperature and seeds do not.
```

Tan et al. [13] find that steerability varies widely across inputs and that steering vectors can fail on some concepts. Turner et al. That is close to our cross-task novelty direction, which transferred perfectly as a readout (AUROC 1.0) but did not raise atypicality monotonically in code (Table 69). STARS [15] and Riemannian activation steering [16] report diversity gains over plain sampling. They do so by optimising several steering directions jointly across concurrent generations at test time, which is a different intervention from one fixed direction. The artifact built the *away-from-mode direction* as the difference in means of commitment-window activations at layers 32 to 34 between non-modal and modal programs, unit-normalised per layer.
